How to tell if you're in starvation mode

I always thought that starvation mode was a real thing until I came here. My sister has been on every diet under the sun--and sometimes was having less than 1200 calories a day and wouldn't lose weight for as long as a week. Eventually she would lose weight if she stuck with it. But a lot of times she'd figure she was in starvation mode and up her calories. What causes that? I want to reverse this myth--but am not sure why everyone believes in starvation mode & why sometimes people stop losing weight for like a week at a time even when they aren't eating a lot of calories.

There is no such thing as starvation mode, otherwise there would be a lot of fat people in Africa. (Time for your science lesson of the day.) The swollen abdomens you see on starving children is actually ascites. Since they're so nutritionally deficient, their bodies lack the capability to produce as much serum proteins as they should have, creating an osmotic imbalance. Fluids that leave the capillaries can no longer be reabsorbed completely, resulting in fluid buildup and swelling.

However, low serum albumin takes quite awhile to manifest and it is NOT the reason people stop losing weight during a diet. The truth of the matter is that they're eating more than they think they are. For a lot of people, it's just little snacks and bites here and there or occasionally larger meals than they should be eating. Whatever the reason, they're getting too many calories.

If you take in more calories than you burn, you gain weight. If you take in the same amount as you burn, your weight doesn't change. If you burn more calories than you eat, you lose weight. Those are the only three options.

Lowering caloric intake is the most important aspect of weight loss. Exercise helps, but it's not the main factor. Remember, you can't outrun your fork.

Adipose cells do not pick up excess water. The human body doesn't spontaneously store water unless something has gone wrong, such as a problem with the kidneys or certain medications that mess up homeostasis in a variety of different ways. For a healthy person, water is excreted at the same rate it's taken in. This is done mostly through the kidneys. When dehydrated, the body will start to conserve water through the use of vasopressin and aldosterone. When thoroughly hydrated, water is simply not reabsorbed by the kidneys and it's quickly excreted. (This actually gets somewhat complicated. I'm not going into the baroreceptors, hormones or brain natriuretic peptide. Nephrology is a pain.)

Basically, unless your kidneys are screwed up or something else has gone wrong, the only water weight you'll hold is however much you drank since the last time you used the bathroom.

While there are a few valid medical reasons for water retention, in 99% of dieters, the issue is that they messed up. Water weight is just another excuse in the plethora of fatlogic for why nothing is their fault.

"water weight" is a real thing, though, vis-à-vis glycogen. Burning up the quick carbs releases the water back into the body and it gets peed out. It's the reason why people will lose weight for a week or so, then stop losing; they were seeing the result of not eating excess carbs.
